source.title: Uncovering the Representation of Spiking Neural Networks Trained with Surrogate Gradient
source.authors: Yuhang Li; Youngeun Kim; Hyoungseob Park; P. Panda

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures representation similarity with CKA between separately trained ANN and SNN models and across different initializations. This is a conceptual test of representation alignment, not the original claim’s broad cross-architecture, cross-objective, or cross-modal scaling test.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper’s reported CKA results that measure ANN–SNN alignment or alignment across initialization seeds. The accuracy figures are not rows because they do not measure representation alignment. The residual-connection ablation’s SNN-with-itself heatmaps and accuracy results do not directly compare ANN–SNN alignment, so they are not separate rows. The clean-versus-adversarial within-model CKA results measure input robustness, not alignment between models, and are also excluded.
record.test_reason: The study measures CKA between separately trained ANNs and SNNs of matching topology while varying width and depth on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and event data. It also compares two seeds of each model type. This is a new setting, a neuron-type change within one topology, with direct results on whether alignment grows with scale (V1), holds across seeds (V3), stays incomplete (V7) and depends on data (V6).
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that surrogate-gradient SNNs learn representations similar to ANNs, higher in wider nets (>0.8 at ResNet-20 ×8) and lower in very deep nets. They find that residual connections regularize SNN representations toward ANN-like ones. The time dimension adds little representation on static data, and event data yields less similar representations. They attribute the similarity to the ANN-like optimization regime and direct encoding of static inputs.
record.recipe_differences: Uses CKA to compare separately trained ANN and SNN representations across layers, sizes, datasets, and seeds; it does not reproduce either named original source’s method. The comparison is primarily between matching network topologies, rather than models differing across architecture, objective, and data.
record.method_sensitivity: Similarity varies with network depth and width, dataset/input type, and layer. CKA curves are described as largely unchanged across the tested SNN time-step counts.

fits_no_version.finding: Residual-branch additions restore ANN–SNN CKA to about 1, while conv and LIF layers lower it. Removing residuals changes SNN self-similarity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architectural skip connections propagate early-layer similarity and drive cross-model alignment in deep nets.

fits_no_version.finding: ANN–SNN CKA is essentially unchanged across SNN time steps from 4 to 128 (also on VGG-13 and CIFAR-100).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adding a temporal dimension to a model does not change its alignment with a non-temporal counterpart on static data.

record.problems: The primary evidence is CKA on selected ANN–SNN pairs, mostly matching topologies and tasks, so it does not establish broad convergence across architectures, objectives, or modalities. Many plotted results have no exact values in the text. The authors describe the study as a pilot study.
record.rows_left_out: No results that directly measure cross-model alignment were left out. Excluded accuracy-only results and within-model clean-versus-adversarial CKA and SNN self-similarity results, which do not measure the claim’s inter-model alignment.

untested.parts: Only ANN vs SNN pairs of identical topology, objective and data are compared. There is no variation across different architectures, objectives, data or modalities, and no large models.
Only two seeds of ResNet-20 are compared. Individual units, bases and features are not compared; CKA only.
No alternative similarity measure or CKA setting is compared. The data effect involves retraining on different data, not a change of evaluation inputs alone.
Shared data or objective is not causally isolated. The authors only argue that a shared optimization regime and direct encoding explain the similarity.

missing.what: CIFAR10-DVS depth and width sweep. ResNet-110 peak CKA is about 0.75 vs about 0.95 on CIFAR-10, and ResNet-20 ×8 has a significantly lower CKA curve than narrower models.
ANN–SNN CKA across permuted seeds is similar in all four permutations and resembles same-model cross-seed heatmaps.
CIFAR-100 time-step sweep and VGG-13 time-step sweep: no CKA differences.
missing.locator: Appendix A.1.2 Fig A.2; A.2 Fig A.7

record.verdict_notes: Both models in each pair share topology, data and objective; only the neuron type (ReLU vs LIF) and the BN variant differ. The V1 bearing is therefore narrow. Width and depth split cleanly: width raises alignment and depth lowers it, even though depth also raises accuracy. Most per-layer values are figure-only.

versions.untested_parts: Tests CKA alignment across width and depth for ANN–SNN pairs on image and event datasets. Does not test broad scaling with independently varying architectures, objectives, data, modalities, or capability across general model families.
No vision–language models or paired image–caption representations.
Compares CKA across two initializations for ANN and SNN ResNet-20s; does not identify individual shared features, units, or bases.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired interchangeability test.
No analysis of recurring interpretable features or circuits.
Shows effects associated with dataset/input type, but does not compare alternative similarity measures or systematically vary CKA settings such as neighbour count.
Reports incomplete or lower alignment in some depths and datasets. It does not causally isolate shared training data or objectives from other possible explanations.

labels.reason: The authors explicitly describe divergence with depth. ResNet-164 has many CKA values below 0.2; the VGG values concern cross-layer comparisons. Improved capability is established for ResNets, not VGGs.

labels.label: limits_scope
labels.condition: Very wide models: ResNet-20 ×16 and ×8 on CIFAR-100
labels.reason: The width trend has layer-dependent qualifications: final-layer differences remain on CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 ×8 results are explicitly irregular. Appendix A.3 separately confirms lower CKA for CIFAR10-DVS ×8 than other widths.

labels.label: supports
labels.condition: Two seeds each of ANN and SNN ResNet-20
labels.reason: Appendix C explicitly reports high CKA between different initializations within each model type.

labels.label: supports
labels.condition: Event datasets CIFAR10-DVS and N-Caltech 101 vs CIFAR-10
labels.reason: Section 4.4 reports dataset-dependent CKA patterns, including a 0.9-to-0.5 decline on CIFAR10-DVS. Training data and input processing change; this is not an isolated evaluation-input or metric comparison.

labels.label: supports
labels.reason: The reported low similarities and explicit divergence support incomplete alignment in these settings. They do not establish a scaling plateau or isolate shared training as its cause.

labels.label: limits_scope
labels.reason: Most layers exceeding 0.8 establishes high similarity, but no threshold establishes near-complete alignment. Remaining final-layer differences are reported, and this result alone does not contradict or qualify V7.

relation.reason: The study directly measures ANN–SNN and cross-seed representation similarity and examines how it changes with width, depth and data.

tranche.reason: Direct representation comparisons extend the question to separately trained artificial and spiking networks, including spatial scaling and event-data settings.

source_check.notes: Figure 2's caption reverses the depth/width signs relative to the explicit results and conclusion; use the body text. Appendix A.3 contains an unlisted width reversal on CIFAR10-DVS at ×8; VGG's 0.3/0.4 values describe cross-layer regions, not uniform corresponding-layer scores.

statements.correction: Section 4.1: wider ANN–SNN pairs have higher CKA; most ResNet-20 ×8 layers exceed 0.8. Section 4.2: selective residual-connection removal and comparisons with/without residual connections. Appendix C: two random seeds for each model type.
statements.problem: The width result and 0.8 value are supported, but the blanket assertion of no reported controls overlooks residual-connection ablations.

statements.correction: Most CIFAR-10 ResNet-20 ×8 layers exceed 0.8 CKA. The width discussion reports remaining differences in the final several layers. No completeness threshold is established.
statements.problem: The high CKA value is correct, but it alone does not establish near-complete alignment or justify limits_scope for V7.
